newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Profits of South Korean companies plunge in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Profits of South Korean companies plunge in 1996.

text.p: The 1996 profits of South Korea's 30 biggest industrial conglomerates were less than one tenth of those in the previous year, but economists said gains were expected this year.

A report by Daishin Economic Research Institute said the 128 listed companies affiliated with the conglomerates posted a combined net profit of 574.5 billion won ($654 million) in calendar 1996, down from 5.79 trillion a year earlier.
The profit drop came despite growth in combined turnover of 16.2 percent to 263.2 trillion won.
The report attributed the poor profits to plunging computer chip prices, huge foreign exchange losses and the Japanese yen's depreciation.
The weaker yen makes Japanese products more competitive with South Korean goods in export markets.
"A fall in global chip prices dragged profits of three major business groups -- Hyundai, Samsung and LG," it said.

Their semiconductor units, Hyundai Electronics Industries Co Ltd, Samsung Electronics Co Ltd and LG Semicon Co Ltd, are the world's leading producers of memory chips used in computers and home appliances, and their performances dictate profitability for the conglomerates.
The sluggish performance of Samsung Group, for example, reflected the dramatic fall in profit at its flagship Samsung Electronics.
Samsung Electronics profit fell to 164 billion won in 1996 from the previous year's 2.5 trillion, causing a 95.5 percent drop in total Samsung Group profit to 125.9 billion won from 2.79 trillion.
Hyundai Group saw its net profits tumble 82 percent to 193.4 billion won last year from 1.09 trillion.
Economists said global chip prices were likely to rebound this year from a freefall last year.
"Voluntary production cutbacks by chipmakers will help improve profits to some degree," said Kim Myung-ho, an economist at Hyundai Securities.
"Prices are already showing signs of improvement," he said.
Unit prices of 16-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips recently edged up to around $9-9.50 in international spot markets from around $6 late last year.

Economists said the tendency of South Korean companies to focus on market share led to poor profits. Many companies also relied on mass-production methods requiring simple technology rather than developing high-tech, higher-value-added goods.
"South Korean companies concentrate on market share rather than profitability," said Park Choon-ho, an economist at Daewoo Economic Research Institute.
"The yen's decline has weakened export competitiveness of automobile, shipbuilding, steel and petrochemical industries," said Park of Daewoo Research.
He said the Korean won's fall against the dollar has also hit companies with large exposure to foreign currency loans.

But Suh Bo-yun, an economist at Dongsuh Securities, said the won's weakness would improve corporate performance this year. "A continuous fall in the won will boost local firms' competitive edge," he said.
Suh saw the won averaging 880 against the dollar this year, falling to 900 in the second quarter and bouncing back to 870 by year-end. Last year, it averaged 804.78.
The won, which closed at 880.00 to the dollar on Monday, has lost 11.97 percent of its value against the U.S. unit since the beginning of last year.
